questions.prompt: What property must a problem have for "binary search on answer" to work?
options: The input array must be sorted in ascending order
The input values must be uniformly distributed
The answer lies in a numeric range and the feasibility condition is monotonic (false…false, true…true)
The function must rise and then fall (unimodal)
questions.explanation: You binary search the answer space instead of an array, which only works if once `IsFeasible(mid)` becomes true it stays true for larger values.

questions.prompt: Interpolation search can reach O(log log n). When does it degrade to O(n)?
options: When the data is skewed or clustered rather than uniformly distributed
When the target is near the start of the array
When the array has an even number of elements
When the array contains negative numbers
questions.explanation: It estimates the target's position from its value, which only works well on uniformly distributed numeric data; skewed data makes the estimates poor and the worst case O(n).

questions.prompt: Which situation is exponential search especially good for?
options: Data where moving backward is expensive
An unsorted array searched only once
Finding the peak of a mountain-shaped function
A sorted sequence whose size is unknown or unbounded
questions.explanation: Exponential search doubles an index (1, 2, 4, 8, …) to find a range and then binary searches it, so it does not need the size up front and is fast when the target is near the start.

questions.prompt: What is ternary search mainly used for?
options: Looking up a value in a sorted array faster than binary search
Finding the maximum or minimum of a unimodal function
Searching unsorted data in O(log n)
Counting duplicates in a sorted array
questions.explanation: Ternary search finds the peak or valley of a function that goes up then down (or down then up). For plain sorted-array lookup, binary search is faster in practice.
